Where participants look before any outcome is visible indicates which locations, and thus which hypotheses about the next attack, they consider. This chapter describes the gaze features computed from the preprocessed fixations (

Features are computed separately for three windows of each trial:
colour cue shown, net placement not yet possible
until the end of the trial
A fixation belongs to the window in which it starts. Positions are drift-corrected, in degrees from the screen centre.
Each colour cue has two target directions, its two latent states; the two cues change state together, and their targets are about 70° apart. The possible outcome locations of a trial are:
target direction of the trial for the shown cue
the other target direction of the shown cue
the direction opposite the circular midpoint of the two states (about 120° from both)
target direction of the other cue in the current latent state
target direction of the other cue in the other latent state
the remaining part of the circle
less than 2.5° from the centre (colour cue)
A fixation 4–12° from the centre is assigned to the nearest of the five directions if it lies within 22.5° (two slots) of it, otherwise to

. Fixations 2.5–4° or more than 12° from the centre are not at a task location. The pairing of the two cues’ targets is read from the episodes (within an episode both cues are in the same latent state). For the 32-slot measures, fixations 5–11° from the centre (the circle of slots) are assigned to the nearest slot.
In this task an event moves the next attack one step, to the other state or to an oddball location:
the current state: the attack comes from here if the state stays;
the other state: after a transition, or an oddball at the other state (57 % of the oddballs);
the third direction: an oddball outside the two states (43 % of the oddballs);
the other cue’s two states: not a possible outcome of the shown cue; gaze there reflects the joint structure of the two cues.

Gaze beyond the current state is the fixation time at the other state, the third direction and the other cue’s states. After an event (t+1, t+2), gaze back at the location of the previous state is analysed with the event measures below.

In the anticipation window of stable trials, participants spend about a quarter of the fixation time at the centre, a quarter to two fifths at the current state and 6–8 % at the other state; the other cue’s states receive 9–16 %. In the prediction window gaze follows the net placement (current state .36 / .41 / .66 in None / Partial / Full). The first fixation outside the centre goes to the other state in 9–11 % of the stable anticipation windows.

Gaze entropy rises with the number of fixations in the window, and participants with higher STICSA state scores make fewer fixations in the anticipation window (−0.45 per SD, p = .038). With log(1 + number of fixations) as a covariate (

), the associations of the anticipation entropy with the scores become smaller and are no longer significant (task locations: STICSA state −0.017, p = .33; STICSA trait −0.024, p = .18; IUS −0.040, p = .068; OCI −0.035, p = .046; general factor −0.026, p = .21; 32 slots all p ≥ .18). In the outcome window they remain (task locations: STICSA trait −0.035, p = .020; STICSA state −0.030, p = .037; general factor −0.030, p = .041). The lower anticipation entropy with higher scores therefore goes together with fewer fixations, i.e. fewer, longer fixations, rather than with a different distribution at the same number of fixations.

Before the outcome of an event trial, gaze in the anticipation and prediction window does not differ between transitions and oddballs (all p ≥ .069): no anticipatory gaze at the location of the coming event.

In the anticipation window, gaze goes to the new location after both event types. After a transition the old location receives slightly more fixation time than after an oddball (+.045, p = .008), the new location does not differ (p = .17): one trial after the event, gaze does not yet separate a change of state from a single oddball.

After a transition, gaze stays at the new location; after an oddball it returns toward the previous state (share at old −.090, new +.21 for transitions vs oddballs, both p < .001; first fixation at old −0.63 log-odds, p = .004). With Full Instructions this separation is larger (transition × Full: old −.20, p < .001; new +.17, p = .002).

the first fixation goes to the old location more often with higher scores (general factor +0.28 log-odds per SD, p = .076; IUS +0.37, p = .015; the IUS slope differs between transitions and oddballs, p = .002; STICSA trait p = .046), while fixation time at the new location is also higher with higher STICSA trait (+.047, p = .010): participants with higher scores first look back at the previous state and then dwell at the new one.

Gaze before and after the placement

(anticipation and outcome window): the associations hold across the three conditions, for the general factor (gaze at slots without nets, outcome entropy, the other state without a net at the outcome) and for the scales, most of them for STICSA trait. Participants with higher scores direct their first fixation to the current state, look less at slots without nets and at the other state when it has no net, and spread their gaze less.

(prediction window): the associations are condition-specific. With Partial Instructions, higher scores go with less gaze beyond the current state; with Full Instructions, higher STICSA state, OCI and general-factor scores go with more gaze at the other state without a net there, and more gaze shifts between the states.
the anxiety-related curvature, direction changes and pull of the first movement are specific to None, and the cursor’s visits to the other state go in opposite directions in None and Full.

Over the task gaze becomes more concentrated: gaze entropy changes by −0.20 bits from episode 1 to 9 in the anticipation window and by −0.12 bits in the outcome window (both p < .001, in every condition). There is also less looking at the other state without a net during the placement (−0.71 log-odds, p < .001), more gaze shifts between the two states (+0.41, p = .031) and slightly more dwell at the current state in the anticipation window (+.045, p = .028). The first mouse movement becomes straighter (curvature −0.28, direction changes −0.35, pull toward the other state −0.086; all p ≤ .002). Gaze reaches the first net location earlier relative to the cursor (+33 ms, p = .033), and splits at t+2 after transitions become rarer (−0.99 log-odds, p = .051; Partial −1.71, p = .024). Much of the change in entropy and in the mouse measures happens between episodes 1 and 2 (
). The first fixation at the current state, gaze at slots without nets, the gaze–cursor lag and following transitions at t+1 do not change (p ≥ .18).

Most questionnaire effects are stable over the task.

They are present in the first half and of similar size in the second half: the first fixation at the current state, less gaze at slots without nets, lower gaze entropy, the gaze lag behind the cursor, the mouse effects in None, the gaze effects of the prediction window in Partial and Full, and the placement strategies after transitions (less following at t+1, more splitting at t+2).

Do participants look back at where something happened on earlier trials, beyond the current trial’s task locations? Two targets are used:

the location of the most recent oddball attack 1–5 trials back, if the attack was shown. The attack of the previous trial lies away from the current task locations almost only when that trial was an oddball (248 of 252 trials), so it is included here at lag 1.
the slots that received nets on the previous trial.

A target counts only if it lies at least 33.75° (the 22.5° task window plus the 11.25° target window) from the current state, the other state and the two states of the other cue of the current trial. The control location is the target mirrored about the current state, so it lies at the same angular distance from the current state. If the mirrored location falls on a task location, the target rotated by +90°, −90° or 180° is used instead; for the nets, all target nets are moved together. Target and control windows are ±11.25° wide at a radius of 4–12°. Replay is the share of fixation time at the target minus the share at the control, in percentage points (pp).

The measure is taken in two windows of the current trial: the anticipation window, before the placement, and the ISI, after the placement and before the outcome. Usable trials: 1,122 trials with an oddball target and 1,432 with a net target, from 87 participants (median 13 per participant for each target). Script:

In the anticipation window 4.4 % of the fixation time falls on the target and 1.9 % on the control (+2.5 pp, p < .001). At least one fixation lands on the target on 19.6 % of trials and on the control on 12.8 % (+0.51 log-odds, p < .001). In the ISI the difference is +2.4 pp (p < .001).

In the anticipation window it is +8.0 pp one trial after the oddball (p < .001), +2.1 pp two trials after (p = .007), and +0.6, +0.3 and +0.2 pp three to five trials after (p ≥ .56). It decreases by −2.0 pp per trial (p < .001). In the ISI the pattern is the same: +5.2 pp, +3.0 pp, then +1.6 pp (p = .056) and less. Because the locations at lags 3–5 are of the same kind as at lags 1–2, the effect is not a general preference for these locations.
Gaze returns to the previous trial’s nets

when they lie away from the current task locations: +3.3 pp in the anticipation window (5.0 % vs 2.2 %, p < .001; at least one fixation 24.8 % vs 13.8 %, +0.73 log-odds, p < .001) and +2.1 pp in the ISI (p < .001).

This holds after stable trials (+3.6 pp, p < .001) and after transitions (+4.7 pp, p = .001; 62 trials of 38 participants), but not after oddballs (+0.2 pp, p = .94; 126 trials of 55 participants). After an oddball, gaze goes to the oddball location instead.
The differences between these trial types are not significant (p ≥ .28).
The control matches the distance from the current state, not the location itself, so this replay may also reflect a preference for the locations a participant tends to use.

Replay of the nets in the anticipation window is larger with Full Instructions (Full vs None + Partial +3.6 pp, p = .007; participant means: None +3.3, Partial +0.6, Full +5.6 pp). For the oddball replay the conditions do not differ (p ≥ .34).
, replay does not change (episode 1 to 9: oddball −2.4 pp, p = .19; nets +0.5 pp, p = .77; ISI p ≥ .48).

Replay is not related to the scores across conditions. General factor: −0.7 to +0.2 pp per SD, p ≥ .24 for both targets and windows. Of the five scales, one slope has p < .05: IUS with the oddball replay in the ISI, −1.1 pp per SD, p = .035. Within conditions, replay of the nets in the ISI increases with STICSA state in None (+2.0 pp per SD, p = .015; differs from Full, p = .016). The replay measure rests on about 13 trials per participant and target, so these participant-level slopes are imprecise.
Higher scores go with relying more on an internal representation of the structure, and with treating surprises as noise until they are confirmed.
This pays off under structural ambiguity (Partial).
With the structure explained (Full), participants with higher scores may consider more hypotheses and end up more uncertain and slower.
How the gaze, gaze–cursor and mouse results relate to each part:

before and after the outcome, gaze of participants with higher scores stays closer to the current state. It shows a first fixation there more often, less gaze at slots without nets, lower gaze entropy, and less looking at the other state when it has no net (general factor and scales, in all three conditions).
the strategies after transitions go the same way: fewer transitions followed at t+1 (general factor −0.26 log-odds, p = .022) and more splits at t+2 (+0.45, p < .001).
at t+2 after a transition the first fixation returns to the previous state more often (general factor +0.28, p = .076; IUS +0.37, p = .015).
these associations are present in the first half of the task.
Does not fit or stays open:
Gaze at the other state in stable phases is not related to the scores.
The lower anticipation entropy goes together with fewer fixations.
Gaze replay of oddball locations does not differ with the scores, so the gaze shows no separate processing of surprises.

Within Partial, higher scores go with more concentrated gaze: less gaze beyond the current state during the placement (general factor −.043, p = .001) and lower anticipation entropy (STICSA state −0.10 bits, p < .001).
Whether this pays off cannot be read from the gaze measures; it depends on the performance measures in the other chapters.
within Full, higher scores go with signs of considering the other state during the placement:
more looking at the other state without a net (general factor +0.42, STICSA state +0.43, OCI +0.45 log-odds);
more gaze shifts between the states (OCI +0.96);
more later nets at the other state (general factor +0.66, p = .019);
a longer gaze lead before the cursor reaches the first net (general factor +33 ms, p = .005).
Gaze entropy before the placement is not higher with higher scores in Full (IUS: lower over the 32 slots).
The gaze associations before and after the placement have the same direction in Full as in the other conditions.
The looking at the other state with STICSA state weakens over the task.

Gaze entropy before the placement is lower with higher STICSA state and trait and OCI scores; this goes together with fewer fixations and is no longer significant when the number of fixations is controlled. In the outcome window gaze entropy is lower with higher STICSA and general-factor scores also with this control. Gaze entropy decreases over the session and does not differ between conditions in the anticipation window. On a given trial, gaze is more spread when the nets are more spread and when the replayed state uncertainty is higher.

Gaze at the other state in stable phases is not related to the instruction condition or to the questionnaire scores, but between participants it goes with the strategies and model parameters that describe treating surprises as noise (noise reactivity) and splitting after transitions. Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Analysis
With higher STICSA trait (and the general factor), gaze goes less often to locations that receive no net, and the first fixation more often to the current state.

The questionnaire associations of the gaze in the anticipation and outcome window hold across the three conditions (same direction, no differences); those in the prediction window are carried by Partial or Full Instructions.

One trial after an event gaze goes to the new location regardless of whether it was a transition or an oddball; transitions and oddballs separate at t+2. With higher IUS the first fixation at t+2 after transitions goes back to the previous state more often. At the outcome of a transition, participants with higher scores look less at their own nets.

Gaze and mouse movement change, mostly between the first and second episode: gaze becomes less spread and the first movement straighter. The questionnaire effects on gaze, the gaze–cursor lag, the mouse (in None) and the strategies after transitions are mostly stable from the first to the second half. None reverses, and the few changes are small.

Gaze returns to the location of an oddball attack on the next one or two trials, and to the previous trial’s nets. This replay does not change over the task and is not related to the questionnaire scores.
